chapter: Chapter 1 — Sexual Reproduction in Flowering Plants
q: Q1. (MCQ) In a plant, the pistil matures several days before the stamens in all flowers. The most important result is that it: (A) guarantees self-pollination (B) promotes autogamy (C) ensures cross-pollination (D) leads to geitonogamy. (SQP 26-27)
a: Answer: (C) It ensures cross-pollination.

chapter: Chapter 1 — Sexual Reproduction in Flowering Plants
q: Q2. (MCQ) An angiosperm embryo sac is located within the: (A) placenta (B) megasporangium (C) nucellus (D) ovary. (2024)
a: Answer: (C) Nucellus.

chapter: Chapter 1 — Sexual Reproduction in Flowering Plants
q: Q3. (MCQ) An anther has 50 microspore mother cells and the ovary has 50 megaspore mother cells. Number of pollen grains and ovules likely formed: (A) 100, 25 (B) 200, 50 (C) 50, 50 (D) 200, 100. (2025)
a: Answer: (B) 200, 50. (Each microspore mother cell → 4 pollen grains by meiosis; each megaspore mother cell → only 1 functional megaspore → 1 embryo sac.)

chapter: Chapter 1 — Sexual Reproduction in Flowering Plants
q: Q4. (2 marks) A mature embryo sac has 7 cells but 8 nuclei. Explain. (2017 OD; similar 2019 D, 2020 D, 2023 D)
a: Answer: The functional megaspore divides 3 times (free nuclear mitosis) → 8 nuclei. 3 nuclei at the micropylar end form the egg apparatus (2 synergids + 1 egg cell); 3 at the chalazal end form 3 antipodal cells; the remaining 2 nuclei (polar nuclei) stay together in one large central cell. So: 3 + 3 + 1 central cell = 7 cells, 8 nuclei.

chapter: Chapter 1 — Sexual Reproduction in Flowering Plants
q: Q5. (3 marks) Explain the monosporic development of the embryo sac. (2023 D; similar 2020 D)
a: Answer: (1) The megaspore mother cell (MMC, 2n) in the nucellus undergoes meiosis → 4 haploid megaspores. (2) 3 megaspores degenerate; only 1 is functional — so it is called monosporic development. (3) The functional megaspore nucleus divides by mitosis 3 times (free nuclear, no walls) → 2, 4, 8 nuclei; then cell walls form → 7-celled, 8-nucleate embryo sac (female gametophyte).

chapter: Chapter 1 — Sexual Reproduction in Flowering Plants
q: Q6. (2 marks) Explain the development of the male gametophyte. Why is it called a male gametophyte? (2023 OD; similar 2017 D, 2025)
a: Answer: The microspore (pollen grain, n) divides by mitosis into a big vegetative cell (food store, irregular nucleus) and a small generative cell (spindle shaped, floats in vegetative cell). In ~60% of angiosperms pollen is shed at this 2-celled stage; in others the generative cell divides again into 2 male gametes (3-celled stage). It is called the male gametophyte because it is the haploid structure that produces the male gametes.

chapter: Chapter 1 — Sexual Reproduction in Flowering Plants
q: Q7. (2–3 marks) List and explain outbreeding devices. (2018 OD, 2023 OD, 2024, 2026)
a:
Answer (any three):

  1. Pollen release and stigma receptivity not synchronised — pollen is released before the stigma is ready, or the stigma is ready much before pollen release (SQP Q1 case).
  2. Anther and stigma at different positions — pollen cannot reach the stigma of the same flower.
  3. Self-incompatibility — a genetic mechanism that stops pollen of the same flower (or plant) from germinating or growing a tube in the pistil.
  4. Unisexual flowers — monoecious plants (castor, maize) prevent autogamy but not geitonogamy; dioecious plants (papaya) prevent both autogamy and geitonogamy.

chapter: Chapter 1 — Sexual Reproduction in Flowering Plants
q: Q8. (2 marks) Geitonogamy can be compared with both cross-pollination and self-pollination. Comment. (SQP 26-27)
a: Answer: Geitonogamy = pollen from the anther of one flower goes to the stigma of another flower of the same plant. Functionally it is like cross-pollination because a pollinating agent is needed; genetically it is like autogamy (self-pollination) because the pollen comes from the same plant.

chapter: Chapter 1 — Sexual Reproduction in Flowering Plants
q: Q9. (3 marks) Explain the steps a plant breeder takes so that only the desired pollen reaches the stigma of a bisexual flower (artificial hybridisation). (2023 D; similar 2015 OD, 2019 OD, SQP 26-27)
a: Answer: (1) Emasculation — remove the anthers from the flower bud with forceps before the anthers dehisce. (2) Bagging — cover the emasculated flower with a butter-paper bag to stop unwanted pollen. (3) When the stigma becomes receptive, dust it with pollen collected from the chosen male parent, and re-bag the flower so the fruit develops. (In unisexual flowers like papaya, no emasculation is needed — only bagging.)

chapter: Chapter 1 — Sexual Reproduction in Flowering Plants
q: Q10. (5 marks) Explain double fertilisation, starting from pollen on the stigma. Give the ploidy of the products and the role of synergids. Why does endosperm develop before the embryo? (2024; similar 2018 OD, SQP 26-27)
a:
Answer:

  • Pollen grain germinates on the stigma → pollen tube grows through the style → enters the ovule through the micropyle → enters one synergid (guided by the filiform apparatus of synergids) → releases 2 male gametes.
  • Syngamy: male gamete 1 + egg cell → zygote (2n) → embryo.
  • Triple fusion: male gamete 2 + 2 polar nuclei in central cell → primary endosperm nucleus, PEN (3n) → endosperm.
  • Two fusions happen in one embryo sac, so it is called double fertilisation.
  • Endosperm develops first because its cells store food, which nourishes the developing embryo. (SQP MS: the statement "zygote always divides before PEN" is false.)

chapter: Chapter 1 — Sexual Reproduction in Flowering Plants
q: Q11. (2 marks) Why do farmers prefer apomictic seeds? (2020 D, 2026; similar 2015 OD, 2019 OD)
a: Answer: Apomixis = formation of seed without fertilisation (example: some Asteraceae and grasses). (1) If a hybrid is made apomictic, the hybrid characters do not segregate in the next generation. (2) So farmers can keep using their own seeds every year instead of buying costly hybrid seeds each year.

chapter: Chapter 1 — Sexual Reproduction in Flowering Plants
q: Q12. (2 marks) When an orange seed is squeezed, many embryos are seen. Explain. Are they genetically similar? (2017 D)
a: Answer: This is polyembryony. In citrus, some nucellar cells around the embryo sac divide and grow into extra embryos (without fertilisation). These nucellar embryos are genetically identical to the mother plant (clones); only the zygotic embryo differs.

chapter: Chapter 1 — Sexual Reproduction in Flowering Plants
q: Q13. (2 marks) Differentiate between true fruit and false fruit, and give an example of a parthenocarpic fruit. (2020 OD; similar 2018 OD, 2026)
a: Answer: True fruit develops only from the ovary (e.g., mango). False fruit — the thalamus also contributes to the fruit (e.g., apple, strawberry, cashew). Parthenocarpic fruit develops without fertilisation and is seedless (e.g., banana).

q: Q14. (MCQ) In humans, the secondary oocyte completes its meiotic division when: (A) it is implanted (B) it is released from the Graafian follicle (C) it is penetrated by the sperm (D) acrosomal enzymes break the zona pellucida. (2024)
a: Answer: (C) When the sperm enters it.

q: Q15. (MCQ) The foetal ejection reflex triggers release of ____ from ____. (A) oxytocin, foetal pituitary (B) oxytocin, maternal pituitary (C) hCG, placenta (D) progesterone, corpus luteum. (2026; similar 2015 D)
a: Answer: (B) Oxytocin, maternal pituitary.

q: Q16. (Assertion–Reason) A: The embryo with 8 to 16 blastomeres is called a morula. R: The morula continues to divide and transforms into trophoblast. (2026)
a: Answer: (C) A is true but R is false. (The morula becomes a blastocyst; trophoblast is only its outer layer.)

q: Q17. (Assertion–Reason) A: Spermatogenesis is continuous throughout a man's reproductive life, while oogenesis is discontinuous. R: Oogenesis begins in the embryo, is arrested at prophase I, resumes after puberty, and is arrested again at metaphase II. (SQP 26-27)
a: Answer: (A) Both true, R is the correct explanation of A.

q: Q18. (2 marks) List the male accessory ducts in order. (2020 OD; 2019 OD diagram; 2024 case)
a: Answer: Rete testis → vasa efferentia → epididymis → vas deferens (→ ejaculatory duct → urethra).

q: Q19. (3 marks) Explain spermatogenesis and the roles of LH and FSH. (2024 case, 2020 D)
a: Answer: In seminiferous tubules: spermatogonia (2n) multiply by mitosis → primary spermatocytes (2n) → meiosis I → secondary spermatocytes (n) → meiosis II → spermatids (n) → change into sperms (spermiogenesis). At puberty the hypothalamus releases GnRH → pituitary releases LH, which acts on Leydig (interstitial) cells to secrete androgens (testosterone) that stimulate spermatogenesis, and FSH, which acts on Sertoli cells to secrete factors that help spermiogenesis.

q: Q20. (3–5 marks) Describe the menstrual cycle phases. (2016 OD, 2019 D, 2025, 2026, SQP 26-27 case)
a:
Answer:

  • Menstrual phase (days 1–5): endometrium breaks down and bleeds out; happens only if the ovum is not fertilised.
  • Follicular/proliferative phase (days ~5–13): FSH and LH rise; primary follicles grow into a mature Graafian follicle; follicle secretes estrogen, which rebuilds the endometrium.
  • Ovulation (about day 14): LH surge causes the Graafian follicle to rupture and release the ovum (secondary oocyte).
  • Luteal/secretory phase (days 15–28): the empty follicle becomes the corpus luteum, which secretes progesterone to keep the endometrium ready for implantation. If no fertilisation, the corpus luteum degenerates → progesterone falls → menstruation starts again. (SQP link: no clear LH surge → no ovulation → no corpus luteum → low progesterone → irregular, heavy bleeding; heavy bleeding can cause anaemia.)

q: Q21. (3–5 marks) Trace the journey of the zygote from the fallopian tube to implantation. (2023 OD; similar 2024, 2025, 2026)
a: Answer: Fertilisation occurs in the ampullary region of the fallopian tube. The zygote divides by mitosis (cleavage) as it moves through the isthmus towards the uterus → 2, 4, 8, 16 daughter cells (blastomeres). Embryo with 8–16 blastomeres = morula. Morula becomes a blastocyst: outer layer trophoblast + inner group of cells, the inner cell mass. The trophoblast attaches to the endometrium; uterine cells divide rapidly and cover the blastocyst → blastocyst gets embedded = implantation → pregnancy. Inner cell mass becomes the embryo; trophoblast helps in nutrition and implantation (SQP Q3).

q: Q22. (2 marks) How is polyspermy prevented? (2024 OR)
a: Answer: When one sperm touches the zona pellucida of the ovum, changes occur in the zona pellucida that block the entry of other sperms.

q: Q23. (2 marks) Why is breast-feeding recommended in the first months? (2016 D, 2018 OD)
a: Answer: The first milk, colostrum, contains many antibodies (IgA) that give the baby passive immunity, and breast milk gives complete nutrition and builds a healthy baby.

q: Q24. (MCQ) A man undergoes an operation in which a small part of the vas deferens is cut and tied. The direct result is: (A) sperm transport into ejaculatory duct and urethra is blocked (B) testosterone stops (C) seminal plasma stops (D) spermatogenesis stops. (SQP 26-27; similar 2023 OD, 2023 D)
a: Answer: (A). This is vasectomy (tubectomy is the similar operation in females).

q: Q25. (2 marks) Name two copper-releasing IUDs and state how they work. (2024; similar 2020 D)
a: Answer: CuT, Cu7, Multiload 375 (any two). Cu ions reduce sperm motility and the fertilising capacity of sperms; IUDs also increase phagocytosis of sperms in the uterus. (Hormone-releasing IUDs like Progestasert and LNG-20 also make the uterus unsuitable for implantation and the cervix hostile to sperms.)

q: Q26. (2 marks) Why is "Saheli" preferred by women? (2020 D)
a: Answer: It is a non-steroidal pill taken once a week, with very few side effects and high contraceptive value. (Developed by CDRI, Lucknow.)

q: Q27. (2 marks) What is amniocentesis? Why is it banned for sex determination? (2026; similar 2019 OD, 2023 D, 2025)
a: Answer: A sample of amniotic fluid around the foetus is taken and tested to detect genetic/chromosomal disorders (such as Down's syndrome). It is legally banned for finding the sex of the foetus because this misuse leads to female foeticide (killing of normal female foetuses).

q: Q28. (2 marks) Why does the government have strict conditions for MTP? (2017 OD)
a: Answer: To stop illegal, unsafe abortions and the misuse of MTP for female foeticide (sex-selective abortion). MTP is safest in the first trimester (up to 12 weeks).

q: Q29. (3 marks) A woman has blocked fallopian tubes but her ovaries make normal ova. Her husband has a very low sperm count. Which ARTs will help? (SQP 26-27; similar 2015 D, 2019 D, 2020 OD, 2023 OD, 2024)
a: Answer: (1) ICSI (Intracytoplasmic Sperm Injection) — a single sperm is injected directly into the ovum in the lab; solves the low sperm count. (2) IVF followed by IUT (Intra Uterine Transfer) — embryo made in the lab (with more than 8 blastomeres) is placed directly into the uterus; this by-passes the blocked fallopian tube.

q: Q30. (3 marks) Expand and explain ZIFT, GIFT and IUI. (2023 OD; similar 2019 D, 2024)
a:
Answer:

  • ZIFT – Zygote Intra Fallopian Transfer: zygote or early embryo (up to 8 blastomeres) made by IVF is put into the fallopian tube.
  • GIFT – Gamete Intra Fallopian Transfer: an ovum from a donor is put into the fallopian tube of a woman who cannot produce ova but can give a suitable environment for fertilisation.
  • IUI – Intra Uterine Insemination (artificial insemination): semen from the husband or a healthy donor is placed into the uterus; used when the man has a low sperm count.

q: Q31. (2 marks) Name any four STIs. Which of them are not completely curable? (NCERT fact; not seen in the papers read — learn as a 2-mark backup)
a: Answer: Gonorrhoea, syphilis, genital herpes, chlamydiasis, genital warts, trichomoniasis, hepatitis B, HIV/AIDS. Hepatitis B, genital herpes and HIV infections are not completely curable.

chapter: Chapter 4 — Principles of Inheritance and Variation
q: Q32. (MCQ) A woman with normal vision has a colour-blind father. She marries a normal man. The chance of their children being colour blind is: (A) 25% (B) 50% (C) 75% (D) 100%. (2024; similar 2025)
a: Answer: (A) 25% of all children (= half of the sons; no daughters affected). Woman is a carrier XᶜX; man XY.

chapter: Chapter 4 — Principles of Inheritance and Variation
q: Q33. (2 marks) You have a tall pea plant. How will you find its genotype? (2019 D; similar 2015 D, 2016 OD, 2017 D, 2023 D)
a:
Answer: Do a test cross: cross it with a dwarf (homozygous recessive, tt) plant.

  • If all offspring are tall → plant is TT (homozygous).
  • If tall : dwarf = 1 : 1 → plant is Tt (heterozygous).

chapter: Chapter 4 — Principles of Inheritance and Variation
q: Q34. (5 marks) Compare inheritance of flower colour in garden pea (violet/white) and snapdragon (red/white) up to F2. (2024, 2025, 2026; similar 2019 OD)
a:
Answer:

  • Pea (complete dominance): VV (violet) × vv (white) → F1 all Vv violet. F1 selfed → F2: VV : Vv : vv = 1 : 2 : 1 (genotype), violet : white = 3 : 1 (phenotype). Violet is dominant.
  • Snapdragon/Antirrhinum (incomplete dominance): RR (red) × rr (white) → F1 all Rr pink. F2: RR red : Rr pink : rr white = 1 : 2 : 1 for both genotype and phenotype.
  • Conclusion: In incomplete dominance neither allele is fully dominant, so F1 shows an intermediate character and the phenotypic ratio equals the genotypic ratio.

chapter: Chapter 4 — Principles of Inheritance and Variation
q: Q35. (3 marks) A woman with blood group O marries a man with blood group AB. Work out the cross and explain the pattern. (2019 D; similar 2015 D, 2025)
a: Answer: Woman ii × Man IᴬIᴮ. Gametes: i and Iᴬ, Iᴮ. Children: Iᴬi (blood group A) and Iᴮi (blood group B) in 1 : 1. No child is O or AB. ABO blood groups show multiple alleles (Iᴬ, Iᴮ, i) and co-dominance (Iᴬ and Iᴮ both express in AB); i is recessive.

chapter: Chapter 4 — Principles of Inheritance and Variation
q: Q36. (3 marks) Mice: running R > walking r; black B > brown b. Cross Rrbb female × RrBb male. Give the phenotypic ratio and number of running-black mice out of 64. (SQP 26-27)
a: Answer: Gametes: female Rb, rb; male RB, Rb, rB, rb. Results: running black 6/16, running brown 6/16, walking black 2/16, walking brown 2/16 → 3 : 3 : 1 : 1. Running black = 6/16 × 64 = 24.

chapter: Chapter 4 — Principles of Inheritance and Variation
q: Q37. (Assertion–Reason) A: Tissue culture is used when traditional breeding cannot keep pace with demand. R: Totipotency is the ability of a single plant cell/explant to regenerate a whole plant under sterile conditions. (SQP 26-27)
a: Answer: (B) Both true, but R is not the correct explanation of A. (One-line extra: a virus-free plant is obtained by culturing the meristem (apical/axillary), which is free of virus — 2026.)

chapter: Chapter 4 — Principles of Inheritance and Variation
q: Q38. (Assertion–Reason) A: When two genes in a dihybrid cross are on the same chromosome, parental combinations are much higher than non-parental. R: This is due to crossing over between the two genes. (2025; similar SQP 26-27)
a: Answer: (C) A is true, R is false. (High parental combinations are due to linkage; crossing over produces the non-parental recombinants.)

chapter: Chapter 4 — Principles of Inheritance and Variation
q: Q39. (3 marks) Explain linkage and recombination from Morgan's work. (2018 OD, 2019 OD, 2020 D)
a: Answer: Morgan worked with Drosophila melanogaster (short life cycle ~2 weeks, many offspring, easy to grow, clear male/female differences, many visible variations). In dihybrid crosses for X-linked genes, F2 ratios differed greatly from 9:3:3:1. Genes on the same chromosome tend to stay together = linkage; new (non-parental) combinations formed by crossing over = recombination. Tightly linked genes (yellow body and white eye) gave very low recombination (1.3%); loosely linked genes (white eye and miniature wing) gave higher recombination (37.2%). Sturtevant used recombination frequency to map gene positions on chromosomes.

chapter: Chapter 4 — Principles of Inheritance and Variation
q: Q40. (2 marks) Explain sex determination in honeybees. Why does a male bee have 16 and a female 32 chromosomes? (2015 OD, 2016 OD, 2020 OD)
a: Answer: Haplodiploid system: a fertilised egg becomes a female (queen or worker), diploid, 32 chromosomes; an unfertilised egg develops by parthenogenesis into a male (drone), haploid, 16 chromosomes. Drones produce sperms by mitosis. Males have no father and cannot have sons, but have a grandfather.

chapter: Chapter 4 — Principles of Inheritance and Variation
q: Q41. (2 marks) How is sex determined in birds and how is it different from humans? (2018 OD; similar 2015 D)
a: Answer: Birds: female is ZW (heterogametic, gives two types of eggs), male is ZZ. Humans: male is XY (heterogametic, two types of sperms), female is XX. So in birds the female decides the sex of the chick; in humans the father's sperm decides it.

chapter: Chapter 4 — Principles of Inheritance and Variation
q: Q42. (2 marks) Why do males suffer from haemophilia more than females? Give two differences between haemophilia and sickle-cell anaemia. (2020 OD, 2024; similar 2017 D)
a: Answer: Haemophilia is X-linked recessive. A male has only one X, so one defective allele makes him ill. A female needs the defective allele on both X chromosomes, which is very rare (mother carrier + father haemophilic). Differences: haemophilia is sex-linked, more males affected, blood does not clot (a clotting protein is missing); sickle-cell anaemia is autosomal recessive, males and females equally affected, caused by glutamic acid → valine change at the 6th position of the β-globin chain (GAG → GUG), RBCs become sickle shaped.

chapter: Chapter 4 — Principles of Inheritance and Variation
q: Q43. (3 marks) How does a single gene mutation cause phenylketonuria (PKU)? What is pleiotropy? (SQP 26-27)
a: Answer: PKU is an autosomal recessive inborn error of metabolism. The person lacks the enzyme that converts phenylalanine to tyrosine. Phenylalanine accumulates and is changed into phenylpyruvic acid and other derivatives; their build-up in the brain causes mental retardation (they are also excreted in urine). Pleiotropy: one gene shows many phenotypic effects (here: mental retardation, reduced hair and skin pigmentation, etc.), because it affects a metabolic pathway.

chapter: Chapter 4 — Principles of Inheritance and Variation
q: Q44. (3 marks) Chromosomal vs Mendelian disorders; describe Down's, Turner's and Klinefelter's syndromes. (2026; similar 2017 OD, 2019 D, 2024, 2025)
a:
Answer: Mendelian disorder = change/mutation in a single gene (haemophilia, sickle cell, thalassemia, PKU, colour blindness). Chromosomal disorder = absence, excess or abnormal arrangement of whole chromosomes, usually due to non-disjunction (failure of chromatids/chromosomes to separate in meiosis).

  • Down's syndrome: trisomy of chromosome 21 (47 chromosomes). Short stature, small round head, furrowed tongue, partially open mouth, broad palm with a characteristic crease, retarded physical, psychomotor and mental development.
  • Klinefelter's syndrome: 44 + XXY (47). Overall masculine but with feminine development (breast development, gynaecomastia), sterile. (Formed when an XX egg is fertilised by a Y sperm.)
  • Turner's syndrome: 44 + XO (45). Female, sterile (rudimentary ovaries), lacks secondary sexual characters.

q: Q45. (MCQ) A DNA molecule is 160 base pairs long and has 30% guanine. How many adenine bases? (A) 48 (B) 64 (C) 96 (D) 192. (2026)
a: Answer: (B) 64. Steps: 160 bp = 320 bases. G = 30%, so C = 30%. A + T = 40%, A = 20%. 20% of 320 = 64.

q: Q46. (MCQ) E. coli grown in ¹⁵N medium is moved to ¹⁴N medium. DNA after 60 minutes (E. coli divides every 20 minutes) will be: (A) 25% hybrid, 75% light (B) 50%/50% (C) 75% hybrid, 25% light (D) 85%/15%. (SQP 26-27; similar 2016 OD, 2016 D, 2020 OD)
a: Answer: (A). Steps: 60 min = 3 generations. Gen 1: all hybrid; Gen 2: ½ hybrid ½ light; Gen 3: ¼ hybrid ¾ light. This proved semi-conservative replication (Meselson and Stahl, 1958, using CsCl density gradient centrifugation).

q: Q47. (MCQ) A stretch of euchromatin has 200 nucleosomes. Number of base pairs? (one nucleosome ≈ 200 bp) (SQP 26-27; similar 2025)
a: Answer: 200 × 200 = 40,000 bp (MS option C: 40,000 bp and 13,600 × 10⁻⁹ m, using 0.34 nm per bp).

q: Q48. (3 marks) Describe the nucleosome and differentiate euchromatin and heterochromatin. (2025; similar 2016 D, 2017 OD)
a: Answer: Histones are positively charged proteins (rich in lysine and arginine). 8 histone molecules form a histone octamer. Negatively charged DNA wraps around it → nucleosome (about 200 bp of DNA). Nucleosomes look like "beads-on-string" under the electron microscope and coil further into chromatin fibres (non-histone chromosomal (NHC) proteins help). Euchromatin = loosely packed, stains light, transcriptionally active. Heterochromatin = densely packed, stains dark, inactive.

q: Q49. (3 marks) Explain Hershey and Chase's experiment. (2015 D, 2019 D; MCQ 2023 OD)
a: Answer: They used bacteriophages. Some phages were grown with radioactive phosphorus ³²P (labels DNA), others with radioactive sulphur ³⁵S (labels protein). (1) Infection: phages infected E. coli. (2) Blending: a blender removed the phage coats from bacteria. (3) Centrifugation: bacteria settled at the bottom; phage coats stayed in the supernatant. Bacteria infected with ³²P phage were radioactive; with ³⁵S phage were not. So DNA, not protein, enters the bacteria — DNA is the genetic material.

q: Q50. (2 marks) Why is DNA a better genetic material than RNA? (2020 OD; A-R 2024, 2023 OD)
a: Answer: RNA has a reactive 2'-OH group in every nucleotide, so it is labile, easily degraded and mutates fast (RNA viruses evolve fast). DNA is chemically more stable (no 2'-OH; thymine instead of uracil), so it is better for storing genetic information. RNA is better for expressing characters (protein synthesis).

q: Q51. (3 marks) Draw a replication fork and explain why replication occurs within a fork. Role of DNA ligase? (2026; similar 2019 OD, 2019 D, 2016 D)
a: Answer: (Diagram in Section 6.) The two DNA strands cannot be separated along the whole length at once because it needs very high energy, so replication happens in a small opening of the helix = replication fork. DNA polymerase works only in the 5'→3' direction, so the template with 3'→5' polarity gives continuous synthesis (leading strand), and the template with 5'→3' polarity gives discontinuous synthesis (lagging strand, short fragments). DNA ligase joins these discontinuous fragments.

q: Q52. (2 marks) Draw/describe a transcription unit. Where are the promoter and terminator? (2019 D, 2019 OD; MCQ 2024, SQP 26-27)
a: Answer: Transcription unit = promoter + structural gene + terminator. The promoter is towards the 5' end (upstream) of the structural gene (with reference to the coding strand); the terminator is towards the 3' end (downstream) of the coding strand. The template strand has 3'→5' polarity; the coding strand has 5'→3' polarity and the same sequence as RNA (T in place of U). In bacteria, RNA polymerase uses the sigma factor to start and the rho factor to stop.

q: Q53. (3 marks) Why must hnRNA be processed? Name the processes. Why is only one DNA strand transcribed? (2026; similar 2017 D, 2023 OD)
a: Answer: In eukaryotes the primary transcript (hnRNA) has both exons (coding) and introns (non-coding). (1) Splicing removes introns and joins exons. (2) Capping: methyl guanosine triphosphate is added at the 5' end. (3) Tailing: 200–300 adenylate residues (poly-A tail) are added at the 3' end. Then it is mRNA and goes to the cytoplasm. Only one strand is copied because (a) if both were copied, the two RNAs would be complementary and pair to form double-stranded RNA, so no protein would be made; (b) two different RNAs/proteins from the same DNA segment would make genetic information transfer complicated.

q: Q54. (2–3 marks) Name the three RNA polymerases in eukaryotes and what each makes. (2023 OD)
a: Answer: RNA polymerase I → rRNAs (28S, 18S, 5.8S); RNA polymerase II → hnRNA (precursor of mRNA); RNA polymerase III → tRNA, 5S rRNA and snRNAs.

q: Q55. (2 marks) When is the genetic code said to be (a) degenerate (b) universal? Also unambiguous? (2020 D; similar 2016 OD, 2017 D, A-R 2025)
a: Answer: (a) Degenerate: some amino acids are coded by more than one codon. (b) Universal: the same codon codes for the same amino acid in all organisms, from bacteria to humans (some exceptions in mitochondria and a few protozoans). Unambiguous/specific: one codon codes for only one amino acid. Other features: triplet; 61 codons for amino acids; 3 stop codons (UAA, UAG, UGA); AUG has a dual role (codes methionine and acts as the start codon); read without commas.

q: Q56. (3 marks) Describe tRNA. Why is it called an adapter molecule? (2017 D; similar 2024, 2023 OD)
a: Answer: tRNA looks like a clover leaf (2-D); in 3-D it looks like an inverted L. It has an anticodon loop (bases complementary to the codon on mRNA) and an amino acid acceptor end (3' end) where a specific amino acid attaches (charging/aminoacylation, which uses ATP). It "reads" the code on mRNA and also carries the matching amino acid, so it is an adapter between nucleic acid and protein. Translation stops when a release factor binds the stop codon. UTRs (untranslated regions) are on mRNA at both the 5' end (before the start codon) and the 3' end (after the stop codon); they are needed for efficient translation.

q: Q57. (5 marks) Explain the lac operon (with inducer and without inducer). (2024 OR, 2025 OR)
a:
Answer: The lac operon of E. coli has a regulator gene i (makes repressor), a promoter (p), an operator (o) and 3 structural genes: z (β-galactosidase), y (permease), a (transacetylase).

  • No lactose (no inducer): the repressor made by the i gene binds to the operator → RNA polymerase cannot transcribe → genes switched off.
  • Lactose present (inducer): lactose (allolactose) binds the repressor and inactivates it → repressor cannot bind the operator → RNA polymerase transcribes z, y, a → enzymes made → lactose is used. Genes switched on.
  • It is called negative regulation because the operon is controlled by a repressor.

q: Q58. (3 marks) Give four goals of the Human Genome Project (HGP). Name one non-human organism sequenced. (2023 D; similar 2020 D, 2017 D)
a: Answer: HGP began in 1990 and was completed in 2003. Goals (any four): identify all the ~20,000–25,000 genes in human DNA; find the sequence of the ~3 billion base pairs; store this information in databases; improve tools for data analysis; transfer related technologies to other sectors such as industries; address the ethical, legal and social issues (ELSI). Non-human organisms sequenced: bacteria, yeast, Caenorhabditis elegans, Drosophila, rice, Arabidopsis (any one).

q: Q59. (5 marks) Describe DNA fingerprinting steps and uses. (2023 D; similar 2015 D, 2017 OD, 2018 OD, 2024 OR)
a: Answer: Technique (Alec Jeffreys) uses VNTRs (Variable Number of Tandem Repeats — a satellite DNA that differs from person to person) as probe. Steps: (1) isolate DNA; (2) digest DNA with restriction endonucleases; (3) separate fragments by gel electrophoresis; (4) transfer (blot) fragments to nitrocellulose/nylon membrane; (5) hybridise with a labelled VNTR probe; (6) detect bands by autoradiography. Uses: forensic science (identify criminals, identify dead bodies after accidents), paternity disputes, studying population and genetic diversity.

q: Q60. (MCQ) Select the odd one in the context of convergent evolution: (A) eyes of octopus and mammals (B) flippers of penguins and dolphins (C) flying squirrel and flying phalanger (D) thorns of Bougainvillea and tendrils of Cucurbita. (2026)
a: Answer: (D) — these are homologous (divergent evolution); the others are analogous/convergent.

q: Q61. (MCQ) If the frequency of allele A is 0.6 in a population in Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium, the frequency of Aa is: (A) 0.21 (B) 0.42 (C) 0.48 (D) 0.32. (2024)
Q62. (2–3 marks) Explain p² + 2pq + q² = 1. Which factors disturb Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium? (2015 OD, 2017 OD, 2018 OD; similar 2020 OD)
a: Answer: Hardy-Weinberg principle: allele frequencies in a population stay constant from generation to generation (genetic equilibrium) if there is no disturbance. p = frequency of dominant allele A, q = frequency of recessive allele a, p + q = 1. Then p² = frequency of AA, 2pq = Aa, q² = aa, and p² + 2pq + q² = 1. Five factors change it: gene migration (gene flow), genetic drift, mutation, genetic recombination, natural selection.

q: Q63. (2 marks) Differentiate homologous and analogous organs with examples. (2016 OD, 2018 OD; similar 2015 OD, 2020 OD, 2024)
a: Answer: Homologous: same basic structure and origin, different functions → divergent evolution (forelimbs of whale, bat, cheetah and human; thorn of Bougainvillea and tendril of Cucurbita; vertebrate hearts/brains). Analogous: different structure/origin, same function → convergent evolution (wings of butterfly and bird; eyes of octopus and mammals; flippers of penguin and dolphin; sweet potato (root) and potato (stem)).

q: Q64. (3 marks) Explain industrial melanism as an example of natural selection. (2023 D; similar 2015 D, 2017 OD)
a: Answer: In England, before industrialisation (before 1850), tree trunks were covered by white lichens, so white-winged moths were hidden from predator birds and were more in number. After industrialisation, smoke and soot darkened the trunks and killed the lichens. Now dark (melanic) moths were hidden and survived, while white moths were eaten → dark moths became more common. Nature selected the better-adapted (fitter) form → natural selection.

q: Q65. (2 marks) Explain adaptive radiation with an example. (2015 D; similar SQP 26-27 continental drift)
a: Answer: Evolution of different species from one ancestor, spreading into different habitats in one geographical area. Examples: Darwin's finches of the Galapagos (different beak types); Australian marsupials, which evolved from one ancestral stock within the island continent. (SQP: due to continental drift, South American mammals were overridden by North American fauna when the continents joined; Australian marsupials survived because there was no competition from other mammals.)

q: Q66. (2 marks) Write the order of human evolution and one feature each. (2025 MCQ, 2023 D MCQ, 2019 OD, 2017 D)
a: Answer: Dryopithecus/Ramapithecus (~15 mya, ape-like) → Australopithecines (~2 mya, East African grasslands, stone weapons, ate fruit) → Homo habilis (first human-like, brain 650–800 cc, probably did not eat meat) → Homo erectus (~1.5 mya, brain ~900 cc, probably ate meat) → Neanderthal man (brain ~1400 cc, used hides to protect the body and buried the dead) → Homo sapiens.

q: Q67. (MCQ) The vector of dengue fever is: (A) female Aedes (B) female Anopheles (C) male Aedes (D) female Culex. (2024; similar 2018 OD)
a: Answer: (A) Female Aedes mosquito (also spreads chikungunya).

q: Q68. (3 marks) "Plasmodium needs both mosquito and human hosts." Explain its life cycle. (2023 D; similar 2023 OD, 2025)
a: Answer: Infected female Anopheles bites a human and injects sporozoites (infective stage). In the human: sporozoites multiply in liver cells, then attack red blood cells, multiply and burst them, releasing haemozoin — a toxin causing chill and high fever every 3–4 days. Some parasites form gametocytes in RBCs. When a female Anopheles sucks this blood, gametocytes enter it; fertilisation and development happen in the mosquito's stomach (gut); sporozoites form and are stored in the mosquito's salivary glands. So the asexual phase is in humans and the sexual phase in the mosquito.

q: Q69. (2 marks each — learn as a table) Disease table. (typhoid 2017 D, 2023 OD; amoebiasis 2016 D; filariasis 2026; ringworm, ascariasis NCERT)
a:
Disease Pathogen Spread Key symptoms
Typhoid Salmonella typhi (bacterium) contaminated food/water high fever 39–40°C, weakness, stomach pain, constipation, headache; Widal test confirms
Pneumonia Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae droplets, sharing glasses alveoli fill with fluid, fever, chills, cough; lips/nails turn grey-bluish
Common cold Rhino viruses droplets, contaminated objects nasal congestion, sore throat, cough (nose & respiratory passage, not lungs)
Malaria Plasmodium (vivax, malariae, falciparum — most serious) female Anopheles chill and high fever every 3–4 days
Amoebiasis Entamoeba histolytica houseflies (mechanical carriers) contaminate food/water constipation, abdominal pain, cramps, stools with mucus and blood clots
Ascariasis Ascaris (roundworm) eggs in soil, water, vegetables internal bleeding, muscular pain, fever, anaemia, blocked intestine
Filariasis (elephantiasis) Wuchereria bancrofti, W. malayi bite of female mosquito (Culex) chronic inflammation and swelling of lymphatic vessels of lower limbs; genitals may be deformed
Ringworm Microsporum, Trichophyton, Epidermophyton (fungi) towels, combs, soil dry scaly lesions on skin, nails, scalp, intense itching; heat and moisture help them grow

q: Q70. (3 marks) Differentiate active and passive immunity; humoral and cell-mediated immunity. (2026, 2024; similar 2019 OD, 2022)
a:
Answer:

  • Active immunity: the body itself makes antibodies after meeting an antigen (infection or vaccine); slow to develop, long-lasting.
  • Passive immunity: ready-made antibodies are given (colostrum IgA from mother; antitoxin for tetanus or snake bite); quick, short-lived.
  • Humoral immunity (antibody-mediated): B-lymphocytes make antibodies that circulate in blood/lymph.
  • Cell-mediated immunity (CMI): done by T-lymphocytes; responsible for graft (organ transplant) rejection. T-cells also help B-cells make antibodies.

q: Q71. (2 marks) Why does a vaccinated child not get the disease? Why don't people get measles/chickenpox twice? (2020 OD, 2016 OD, 2019 D)
a: Answer: The vaccine (weakened/killed pathogen or its proteins) or first infection produces a primary response and also memory B and T cells. On the next exposure, these memory cells quickly produce a massive secondary (anamnestic) response that destroys the pathogen before disease develops.

q: Q72. (2 marks) Explain cytokine barriers and the role of the spleen. (2018 OD, 2025; spleen 2026)
a: Answer: Cytokine barrier: virus-infected cells secrete proteins called interferons, which protect non-infected cells from further viral infection. Spleen: a large bean-shaped secondary lymphoid organ with lymphocytes and phagocytes; it filters blood by trapping blood-borne microorganisms and is also a large reservoir of erythrocytes.

q: Q73. (4 marks — case) Which cells does HIV attack? What happens inside? Test used? (2024 case; similar 2019 D, 2020 OD, 2020 D)
a: Answer: HIV (a retrovirus with RNA) first enters macrophages: the enzyme reverse transcriptase makes viral DNA from viral RNA; viral DNA joins the host cell's DNA and the infected cell makes new viruses (macrophage becomes an "HIV factory"). HIV then enters helper T-lymphocytes (TH cells), multiplies and kills them, so the number of helper T cells falls → immunodeficiency → the patient dies from other (opportunistic) infections such as bacteria, viruses, fungi and Toxoplasma. Test: ELISA (Enzyme Linked Immuno-Sorbent Assay). Treatment: anti-retroviral drugs, only partly effective (prolong life). Prevention: screen blood, use disposable needles and syringes, safe sex/condoms, awareness (NACO).

q: Q74. (3 marks) Differentiate addiction and dependence. Why does a user increase the dose over time? Also name the source of heroin. (SQP 26-27; similar 2018 OD, 2020 D, 2024, 2025)
a: Answer: Addiction = psychological attachment to the "high"/euphoria of a drug, even when it is not needed. Dependence = the body's physical need for the drug; stopping it causes withdrawal symptoms (anxiety, shakiness, nausea, sweating). Repeated use raises the tolerance of body receptors, so they respond only to higher doses. Heroin ("smack", diacetylmorphine) is made by acetylation of morphine, which comes from the latex of the poppy Papaver somniferum; it is a depressant. Cannabinoids (Cannabis sativa) affect the cardiovascular system; cocaine (Erythroxylum coca) interferes with dopamine transport and is a stimulant.

q: Q75. (2–3 marks) Name the microbe used for each product. (2015 D, 2016 D, 2017 D, 2019 D, 2022, 2026, MCQ 2024)
a:
Answer (learn this table):

Product Microbe
Curd Lactobacillus (LAB) — also increases vitamin B12, checks disease-causing microbes in stomach
Bread, ethanol, wine, beer Saccharomyces cerevisiae (baker's/brewer's yeast)
Swiss cheese (large holes) Propionibacterium sharmanii — holes due to large amount of CO₂
Citric acid Aspergillus niger (fungus)
Acetic acid Acetobacter aceti (bacterium)
Butyric acid Clostridium butylicum (bacterium)
Lactic acid Lactobacillus
Penicillin Penicillium notatum (Fleming; Chain and Florey showed its full use)
Streptokinase ("clot buster" for heart attack) Streptococcus
Cyclosporin A (immunosuppressant for organ transplant) Trichoderma polysporum (fungus)
Statins (lower blood cholesterol by inhibiting the enzyme for cholesterol synthesis) Monascus purpureus (yeast)

Whisky, brandy, rum are made with distillation; wine and beer without distillation (2025).

q: Q76. (3 marks) Explain secondary (biological) treatment of sewage. What is BOD? (2017 D; similar 2015 OD, 2016 D, 2017 OD, 2019 OD, 2022)
a: Answer: Primary effluent goes into large aeration tanks, where it is constantly agitated mechanically and air is pumped in → useful aerobic microbes grow into flocs (masses of bacteria with fungal filaments). They consume most of the organic matter, so BOD falls. The effluent then goes to a settling tank, where flocs settle = activated sludge. A small part is pumped back to the aeration tank as inoculum; the major part goes to anaerobic sludge digesters, where anaerobic bacteria digest it and produce biogas (methane, hydrogen sulphide, CO₂). The treated effluent is released into rivers. BOD (Biochemical Oxygen Demand) = the amount of oxygen that would be consumed if all the organic matter in one litre of water were oxidised by bacteria; higher BOD = more polluted water. (SQP A-R: the aim of sewage treatment is to reduce organic matter; high BOD means more, not less, organic matter.)

q: Q77. (2 marks) Biogas: which microbes, where found, which institutes developed the technology? (2023 OD; similar 2015 OD, 2019 OD, 2022)
a: Answer: Methanogens (e.g., Methanobacterium) grow anaerobically on cellulose and produce methane with CO₂ and H₂. Found in anaerobic sludge during sewage treatment and in the rumen of cattle (so cattle dung, "gobar", is used). The technology was developed in India mainly by IARI (Indian Agricultural Research Institute) and KVIC (Khadi and Village Industries Commission).

q: Q78. (3 marks) Why are baculoviruses (Nucleopolyhedrovirus) good biocontrol agents? Name other biocontrol agents and biofertilisers. (SQP 26-27 case; similar 2016 OD, 2020 OD, 2022, 2023 D)
a: Answer: Baculoviruses (genus Nucleopolyhedrovirus) attack insects and arthropods. They are species-specific, narrow-spectrum insecticides with no negative effect on plants, mammals, birds, fish or non-target insects — so they are ideal for Integrated Pest Management (IPM) and ecologically sensitive areas. Other biocontrol agents: ladybird (eats aphids), dragonflies (mosquitoes), Bacillus thuringiensis (spores sprayed on plants kill butterfly caterpillars — toxin is released in the larval gut), Trichoderma (free-living fungus in root ecosystems, controls plant pathogens). Biofertilisers: Rhizobium (root nodules of legumes, fixes N₂), Azospirillum and Azotobacter (free-living N₂ fixers), mycorrhiza such as Glomus (absorbs phosphorus from soil, gives resistance to root pathogens, tolerance to salinity and drought — SQP Q12), cyanobacteria Anabaena, Nostoc, Oscillatoria (fix N₂ in paddy fields, add organic matter).

q: Q79. (MCQ) Which is NOT a feature of plasmids? (A) circular (B) self-replicating (C) single-stranded (D) extra-chromosomal. (2024)
a: Answer: (C) Plasmids are double-stranded.

q: Q80. (Assertion–Reason) A: Chitinase is needed to separate DNA from yeast cells but not from Spirogyra. R: Fungal cell wall is made of chitin. (2026; similar 2024, SQP 26-27)
a: Answer: (A) Both true, R explains A. (Use lysozyme for bacteria, cellulase for plant/algal cells, chitinase for fungi.)

q: Q81. (3 marks) Explain naming of restriction enzymes and formation of recombinant DNA using EcoRI. (2019 D; similar 2017 D, 2019 OD, 2020 OD, 2025)
a: Answer: EcoRI: E = genus Escherichia, co = species coli, R = strain RY13, I = first enzyme isolated from this strain. Restriction endonucleases recognise a palindromic sequence (reads the same on both strands in the 5'→3' direction), e.g. EcoRI site: 5'–GAATTC–3' 3'–CTTAAG–5' EcoRI cuts between G and A on both strands, a little away from the centre, leaving single-stranded overhangs = sticky ends. If the vector and the foreign DNA are cut with the same enzyme, they have matching sticky ends, which pair by hydrogen bonds; DNA ligase then seals them → recombinant DNA.

q: Q82. (3 marks) In pBR322, state the role of ori, ampR/tetR, rop and restriction sites. Explain insertional inactivation. (2020 OD, 2024, 2026 case; similar 2016 OD, 2019 D, 2023 OD, SQP 26-27)
a: Answer: ori — origin of replication; any DNA linked to it can replicate in the host and it controls the copy number. ampR and tetR — antibiotic-resistance genes (ampicillin, tetracycline) used as selectable markers to identify transformants. rop — codes for proteins involved in replication of the plasmid. Restriction sites — single sites (EcoRI, HindIII, ClaI, PvuII, BamHI, SalI, PstI, PvuI) where foreign DNA can be inserted. (BamHI and SalI are in tetR; PstI and PvuI in ampR; PvuII in rop.) Insertional inactivation: foreign DNA is inserted into one marker gene, e.g., tetR at BamHI — that gene stops working. Recombinants grow on ampicillin but not on tetracycline; non-recombinants grow on both. Easier method: insert the foreign DNA into the β-galactosidase gene — recombinants give colourless/white colonies; non-recombinants give blue colonies on a chromogenic substrate.

q: Q83. (2 marks) How are bacteria made competent? Name two vector-less methods of gene transfer. (2026, 2024; similar 2016 OD, 2025)
a: Answer: DNA is hydrophilic and cannot pass cell membranes. Bacterial cells are treated with a specific concentration of a divalent cation, calcium (Ca²⁺), then placed on ice, given a heat shock (42°C) and put back on ice → recombinant DNA enters. Vector-less methods: microinjection (DNA injected directly into the nucleus of an animal cell); biolistics/gene gun (plant cells bombarded with high-velocity gold or tungsten micro-particles coated with DNA).

q: Q84. (3 marks) Explain gel electrophoresis. (2025; similar 2016 D, 2017 OD, 2024)
a: Answer: DNA fragments are negatively charged, so in an electric field they move towards the anode through agarose gel (from seaweed). The gel acts as a sieve: smaller fragments move farther. Separated DNA is stained with ethidium bromide and seen as bright orange bands under UV light. The bands are cut out and the DNA extracted (elution), then used to make recombinant DNA by joining with cloning vectors, in DNA fingerprinting, etc.

q: Q85. (3 marks) Describe PCR. Role of Taq polymerase? (2017 D; similar 2015 OD, 2016 D, 2019 OD, 2023 D, 2023 OD)
a: Answer: PCR = Polymerase Chain Reaction, used to make many copies of a gene in vitro. Each cycle: (1) Denaturation — high temperature separates the two DNA strands. (2) Annealing — two sets of primers (small, chemically synthesised oligonucleotides) bind to complementary regions. (3) Extension — DNA polymerase extends the primers using nucleotides. Repeating ~30 times amplifies the DNA about 1 billion times. Taq polymerase is a thermostable DNA polymerase from the bacterium Thermus aquaticus; it stays active at the high temperature of denaturation, so new enzyme need not be added in every cycle.

q: Q86. (2 marks) Why are bioreactors used? Describe a stirred-tank bioreactor. (2018 OD; similar 2015 D, 2019 OD, 2023 D, 2025)
a: Answer: Bioreactors (100–1000 litres) allow large-scale production of products by providing optimum growth conditions (temperature, pH, substrate, salts, vitamins, oxygen). Stirred-tank bioreactor: usually cylindrical with a curved base for mixing; a stirrer mixes contents evenly and increases oxygen availability; in the sparged type, sterile air is bubbled in. It also has a foam-control system, temperature and pH control, and sampling ports. (SQP: a fall in yield due to contamination is prevented by sterile handling, sterilised equipment and aseptic transfer.)

q: Q87. (3 marks) How was human insulin made by rDNA technology? (2015 OD, 2015 D, 2017 D; similar 2018 OD, 2020 OD)
a: Answer: Insulin has two short chains, A and B, joined by disulphide bridges. In the body it is made as pro-insulin, which has an extra stretch, the C-peptide, that is removed to make mature insulin. In 1983 Eli Lilly prepared two DNA sequences for chains A and B, introduced them into plasmids of E. coli, produced the chains separately, extracted them and combined them by creating disulphide bonds → human insulin (Humulin). It avoids allergy/reactions caused by insulin from cattle or pigs.

q: Q88. (2–3 marks) Explain gene therapy for ADA deficiency. Why is periodic infusion needed? (2025; similar 2015 OD, 2016 OD, 2019 OD)
a: Answer: Adenosine deaminase (ADA) is needed for the immune system; its deficiency (deletion of the ADA gene) causes immunodeficiency. In 1990 a 4-year-old girl was treated: her lymphocytes were grown in culture, a functional ADA cDNA was introduced into them using a retroviral vector, and the cells were returned to her body. These lymphocytes are not immortal, so periodic infusion is needed. Permanent cure: introduce the ADA gene isolated from bone-marrow cells into cells at early embryonic stages. (Other options: bone-marrow transplant, enzyme replacement therapy — injecting functional ADA.)

q: Q89. (3 marks) How was Bt cotton made pest resistant? Why does the Bt toxin not kill the bacterium? (2023 D; similar 2017 D, 2017 OD, 2020 D, 2020 OD, 2022, 2024 OR)
a: Answer: Bacillus thuringiensis makes Bt toxin protein crystals that kill certain insects (lepidopterans like bollworms, coleopterans, dipterans). The toxin exists as an inactive protoxin, so the bacterium is not harmed. When an insect eats it, the alkaline pH of the insect gut dissolves the crystals and activates the toxin; the active toxin binds to the surface of midgut epithelial cells, makes pores, cells swell and burst (lyse) → insect dies. The toxin is coded by cry genes; cryIAc and cryIIAb control cotton bollworms, cryIAb controls corn borer. These genes were introduced into cotton → Bt cotton.

q: Q90. (3 marks) How was tobacco made resistant to the nematode Meloidegyne incognitia? (2024; similar 2016 D, 2018 OD, 2023 OD, MCQ 2025, SQP 26-27)
a: Answer: The nematode infects tobacco roots and reduces yield. Using Agrobacterium vectors, nematode-specific genes were introduced into tobacco so that the plant made both sense and anti-sense RNA. These two complementary RNAs formed double-stranded RNA (dsRNA), which started RNA interference (RNAi): it silenced the specific mRNA of the nematode (stopped its translation). So the parasite could not survive in the transgenic plant.

q: Q91. (3 marks) List benefits of GM plants. Give uses of transgenic animals. (2016 D, 2019 OD, 2020 D, 2026; similar 2015 OD)
a: Answer: GM plants: (1) more tolerant to abiotic stresses (cold, drought, salt, heat); (2) less use of chemical pesticides (pest-resistant crops); (3) fewer post-harvest losses; (4) better use of minerals by plants (prevents early exhaustion of soil fertility); (5) more nutritional value — e.g., Golden rice, rich in vitamin A. Transgenic animals: study of normal physiology and development; study of diseases; biological products (e.g., α-1-antitrypsin for emphysema; transgenic cow Rosie (1997) gave human-protein-enriched milk, 2.4 g/L α-lactalbumin); vaccine safety testing (e.g., polio vaccine on transgenic mice); chemical safety (toxicity) testing.

q: Q92. (1–2 marks) What is biopiracy? What is GEAC? (2015 D, 2016 OD, 2017 OD; MCQ 2025)
a: Answer: Biopiracy = use of bio-resources (and traditional knowledge) of a country by multinational companies or other organisations without proper authorisation from, or compensation to, the countries and people concerned (e.g., an American company got a patent on Basmati rice in 1997). GEAC = Genetic Engineering Approval Committee (Indian government body that decides on the validity of GM research and the safety of introducing GM organisms for public use).

q: Q93. (MCQ) An interaction where one species benefits and the other is neither harmed nor benefited: (A) mycorrhiza (B) sea anemone and clownfish (C) Abingdon tortoise and goats (D) Cuscuta on hedge plants. (2026)
a: Answer: (B) Commensalism.

q: Q94. (3 marks — learn as a table) Population interactions with examples. (2016 OD, 2019 OD, 2023 D, 2023 OD, 2024, 2026; SQP 26-27)
a:
Interaction Sign Example
Mutualism + / + lichen (fungus + alga); mycorrhiza (fungus + plant roots); fig tree and wasp; orchid Ophrys and bee (pseudocopulation); plant and pollinator
Competition − / − Abingdon tortoise and goats in Galapagos (tortoises became extinct)
Predation + / − tiger–deer; Monarch butterfly is distasteful to predators due to a chemical it gets as a caterpillar by feeding on a poisonous weed
Parasitism + / − Cuscuta on hedge plants; brood parasitism — cuckoo (koel) lays eggs in a crow's nest; eggs look similar, so the crow incubates them
Commensalism + / 0 orchid growing on a mango branch; barnacles on whale; cattle egret and grazing cattle; sea anemone and clownfish
Amensalism − / 0 one harmed, other unaffected

Gause's competitive exclusion principle (2026): two closely related species competing for the same limited resources cannot coexist indefinitely; the competitively inferior one is eliminated. (MacArthur's warblers coexist by resource partitioning — feeding in different parts of the tree.) Plant defence (2023 D): cattle and goats do not browse Calotropis because it makes highly poisonous cardiac glycosides. Other plants have thorns (Acacia, cactus) as mechanical defence. Positive roles of predators (2024): pass energy across trophic levels; keep prey populations under control (prickly pear cactus in Australia was controlled by a cactus-feeding moth); maintain species diversity by reducing competition among prey (removing the starfish Pisaster led to extinction of more than 10 invertebrate species).

q: Q95. (3 marks) Name population attributes, draw age pyramids and give growth equations. (2017 OD, 2020 OD, 2022, 2025; similar 2015 OD, 2016 OD, 2017 D, 2019 D)
a: Answer: Attributes of a population (not of an individual): birth rate (natality), death rate (mortality), sex ratio, age distribution. Age pyramids: expanding (triangular — many young, growing population), stable (bell-shaped), declining (urn-shaped — fewer young). Density measured by counting, per cent cover, pug marks and fecal pellets (tigers), catch per trap (fish). Growth: Nₜ₊₁ = Nₜ + [(B + I) − (D + E)]. Exponential growth dN/dt = rN gives a J-shaped curve (unlimited resources). Logistic growth dN/dt = rN[(K − N)/K] gives an S-shaped (sigmoid) curve; K = carrying capacity. r = intrinsic rate of natural increase. Example (2025): if density at t + 1 = 800, natality 200, immigration 200, mortality 150, emigration 100 → 800 = Nₜ + (200 + 200) − (150 + 100) → Nₜ = 650. Example (2019 D): 100 frogs, 20 born in a year → birth rate = 20/100 = 0.2 offspring per frog per year.

q: Q96. (2 marks) Differentiate GPP and NPP. Calculate NPP when GPP = 3500 and R = 1300 g/m²/year. (SQP 26-27; similar 2025, 2017 D, 2015 D)
a: Answer: GPP (gross primary productivity) = rate of production of organic matter in photosynthesis. NPP = GPP − R (respiration losses); it is the biomass available to consumers (herbivores and decomposers). NPP = 3500 − 1300 = 2200 g/m²/year. Productivity is expressed in g m⁻² yr⁻¹ or (kcal m⁻²) yr⁻¹.

q: Q97. (5 marks) Explain the steps of decomposition and factors affecting it. (SQP 26-27 OR; similar 2020 D, 2024, A-R 2023 D, MCQ 2025)
a: Answer: (1) Fragmentation — detritivores (earthworm, termites) break detritus into small particles. (2) Leaching — water-soluble inorganic nutrients go down into the soil and get precipitated as unavailable salts. (3) Catabolism — bacterial and fungal enzymes break detritus into simple inorganic substances. (4) Humification — forms humus, dark amorphous material, highly resistant to microbial action, decomposes very slowly; it is a reservoir of nutrients. (5) Mineralisation — humus is further broken by microbes to release inorganic nutrients. Factors: decomposition is slow if detritus is rich in lignin and chitin, fast if rich in nitrogen and water-soluble sugars; warm and moist conditions speed it up; low temperature, dryness and anaerobic conditions slow it.

q: Q98. (2–3 marks) Differentiate grazing and detritus food chains. Why is the pyramid of biomass in the sea inverted? Limitations of ecological pyramids? (2026; MCQ 2024)
a: Answer: GFC starts from green plants (producers), energy source is the sun (grass → goat → man). DFC starts from dead organic matter, with decomposers (fungi, bacteria — saprotrophs). In aquatic ecosystems GFC carries more energy; in terrestrial ecosystems more energy flows through DFC. Sea: biomass of fishes is more than that of phytoplankton (which reproduce fast but are small) → inverted biomass pyramid. The pyramid of energy is always upright. Limitations: (1) does not consider the same species at two or more trophic levels; (2) assumes a simple food chain, not a food web; (3) saprophytes/decomposers are not given any place.

q: Q99. (MCQ) Which fish led to the extinction of more than 200 species of cichlid fish in Lake Victoria? (A) Catla (B) Dogfish (C) Nile perch (D) African catfish. (2026)
a: Answer: (C) Nile perch.

q: Q100. (3 marks) Explain the three levels of biodiversity with examples. (2026; similar 2016 D, 2018 OD)
a: Answer: Genetic diversity — variation within a species: Rauwolfia vomitoria in the Himalaya differs in potency/concentration of reserpine; India has more than 50,000 strains of rice and 1,000 varieties of mango. Species diversity — variety of species: the Western Ghats have more amphibian species than the Eastern Ghats. Ecological diversity — variety of ecosystems: India has deserts, rainforests, mangroves, coral reefs, wetlands, estuaries and alpine meadows, so it has more ecosystem diversity than Norway.

q: Q101. (4–5 marks) Explain the causes of biodiversity loss ("Evil Quartet"). (SQP 26-27; similar 2017 OD, 2019 D, 2020 OD, 2025)
a:
Answer:

  1. Habitat loss and fragmentation — most important cause; e.g., tropical rainforests once covered 14% of Earth's land, now only 6%; the Amazon is being cleared for soybean and cattle ranches. Fragmentation hurts animals that need large territories and migratory animals.
  2. Over-exploitation — e.g., Steller's sea cow and passenger pigeon became extinct due to over-exploitation by humans; many marine fish are over-harvested.
  3. Alien species invasions — Nile perch in Lake Victoria (200+ cichlid species lost); carrot grass (Parthenium), Lantana and water hyacinth (Eichhornia); African catfish Clarias gariepinus threatens native catfishes in Indian rivers.
  4. Co-extinctions — when a species becomes extinct, plants and animals obligately linked to it also become extinct (e.g., a host fish and its parasites; plant–pollinator mutualism). IUCN Red List (2004): 784 species became extinct in the last 500 years (338 vertebrates, 359 invertebrates, 87 plants). Recent extinctions: dodo (Mauritius), quagga (Africa), thylacine (Australia), Steller's sea cow (Russia), three subspecies of tiger (Bali, Javan, Caspian).

q: Q102. (3–5 marks) Explain in-situ and ex-situ conservation. What are hotspots and sacred groves? (2016 D, 2017 OD, 2019 OD, 2025; similar 2015 OD, 2019 D, MCQ 2023 OD)
a: Answer: In-situ (on site): protect species in their natural habitat — biodiversity hotspots (regions with very high species richness and high endemism; 34 in the world; India has 3 that also cover neighbouring countries: Western Ghats and Sri Lanka, Indo-Burma, Himalaya; hotspots cover less than 2% of the earth's land area), protected areas like biosphere reserves, national parks and wildlife sanctuaries, and sacred groves (forest patches protected by tribal communities for religious reasons — Khasi and Jaintia Hills in Meghalaya, Aravalli Hills of Rajasthan, Western Ghats of Karnataka and Maharashtra, Sarguja, Chanda and Bastar areas of MP/Chhattisgarh). Note: Jaintia Hills are a sacred grove area, not a hotspot (2023 OD MCQ). Ex-situ (off site): threatened species taken out of the habitat and protected in zoological parks, botanical gardens, wildlife safari parks, and by cryopreservation of gametes, in vitro fertilisation, tissue culture, and seed banks. IUCN Red Data List records threatened and extinct species and helps decide conservation priorities.

q: Q103. (3 marks) Why should we conserve biodiversity? (2023 D; similar 2016 D)
a:
Answer: (1) Narrowly utilitarian: humans get food (cereals, pulses, fruits), firewood, fibre, construction material, industrial products (tannins, lubricants, dyes, resins, perfumes) and medicines (more than 25% of drugs sold come from plants); bioprospecting looks for useful products. (2) Broadly utilitarian: ecosystem services — the Amazon forest produces about 20% of the Earth's oxygen through photosynthesis; pollination by bees, birds and bats; aesthetic pleasure. (3) Ethical: every species has an intrinsic value; we have a moral duty to care for them and pass them on to future generations.
